newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels enter Zaire's second city to cheers.
newsitem.headline: Rebels enter Zaire's second city to cheers.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's rebels entered Lubumbashi in triumph on Wednesday, cheered as liberators in Zaire's second city, their biggest prize to date.
Crowds cheered "Kabila, Kabila" as the rebels arrived in the southern suburbs from the direction of the Zambian border. One man did cartwheels and handstands of joy in the street.
The highest civilian authority in the copper mining centre, Shaba provincial governor Kyungu wa Kumwanza, told Reuters by telephone that he was waiting at his home for the rebels to contact him.

"If they ask me, I see no reason not to cooperate with them. If the people are happy, I am happy too. And they are happy, they are celebrating," said Kumwanza, appointed two weeks ago by the tottering President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Residents contacted by telephone said at 3.30 p.m. (1330 GMT) the rebels had not yet entered the post office square that marks the city centre, though Zairean soldiers were nowhere to be seen and there had been no sign of looting.
Firing died away after four p.m.
"It's calm, people are leaning on their balconies waiting for the rebels to come," said one woman contacted by telephone in the city centre.

Rebels said they had met fierce resistance some 15 km (10 miles) out of town, after which they had marched in. One commander said he had two wounded men. There had been heavy mortar and gunfire through the early afternoon.
Government soldiers, who many had feared would put up a fight, seemed to have fled in stolen vehicles towards the airport some six km (four miles) northeast of town.
Late on Wednesday afternoon a white aircraft landed at the airport. An airport source said government troops were still in control there and the jet was due to evacuate a general.
"We are fighters who have come to liberate you," one rebel soldier told gleeful staff at the city's top hotel, the Karavia, which lies three km (two miles) south of the post office.

"There is no problem, do not be afraid, we are here to protect you," he said to applause and smiles from doormen and waiters. He spoke Swahili, the lingua franca of East Africa, but not much French, the national language of Zaire.
The staff provided fizzy red soda pop to quench the thirst of the more than a dozen rebels lined up around the hotel.

They wore white headbands from ripped up tablecloths, a symbol of support for Kabila's Alliance of Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire which now controls all major cities but the nervous capital, Kinshasa, 1,800 km (1,200 miles) away.
"We are too happy, too happy. We were colonised for 35 years by that dictator Mobutu. He looted our Katanga," said Henri Kisimuzima, 48, security chief at the hotel.
"We hope Katanga will now be free, as an independent country or in a federation." Katanga is the old name for Shaba province, one of dozens of place names changed by Mobutu.
The hotel staff first donned their white bandannas on Monday as news spread that rebels, appearing from nowhere, had taken Kipushi on the Zambian border, a mere 30 km (20 miles) away.
Some of the city's soldiers changed sides the same day.

The staff stuffed their bands back into their pockets when it became clear the rebels were being held up by diehard members of Mobutu's Special Presidential Division DSP, who had been flown in and ordered to fight.
"We had a serious encounter at Lion's Hill, about 15 km from here. But once we broke the resistance there, we just moved ahead," said one rebel, in the Kabila uniform of olive fatigues and boots.
Gloom had spread across Lubumbashi on Tuesday as it became clear that the rebels would not sail into town unopposed.
People began to fear that the dreaded DSP, trapped it seemed by rebel advances from three or four directions, might be cornered and forced into a bloody last stand.
It was not clear where they had headed after fleeing the army headquarters, near the Karavia, and from other places where the rebels were advancing.
Crowds of civilians flocked into the deserted barracks in carnival mood and helped themselves to corn and vegetables being grown to feed the departed soldiers.
"This is not looting, we are just taking back what the army stole from us over 30 years," said one of those picking corn cobs, Christian Kakinga.
People in the crowd said many soldiers had stripped off their uniforms and dumped them before fleeing the rebel advance.
Electricity and the city's main cellular telephone network, both of which went off in previous battles for cities, were still working in Lubumbashi even after the rebels came.
